reading.title: Turning Old Rail Lines into Green Parks
reading.purpose: Discover how cities redesign unused industrial spaces into parks for everyone.
paras: In many cities, old train tracks and brick depots sit empty long after freight trains leave. Instead of tearing everything down, city planners often convert these empty strips into public parks and bike trails. Turning steel and gravel into shade trees takes care. Old rail sites can carry adverse conditions, harmful problems like hard soil or poor drainage that work against young plants.

Before planting begins, crews must handle rainwater. Heavy storms once flooded the tracks. Now workers dig shallow basins that divert runoff away from nearby homes and into rain gardens. This simple shift helps avert costly flood damage during spring storms. Designers also try to invert the old role of the tracks: a strip that once split two blocks becomes a green path that links them.

Such projects rarely happen without controversy, a loud public debate in which neighbors argue over costs, parking, and noise. Some people worry that rising rents could reverse the work of keeping the area affordable. Others fear that without steady care, a fresh trail might revert to a weedy lot full of trash. Open meetings let critics and fans trade ideas until a better plan takes shape.

When the work goes well, a long narrow park proves very versatile, able to serve many uses in one tight space. Morning riders pedal past small gardens, while families meet near play spots. Even an introvert who prefers quiet time alone can find a shaded bench tucked behind tall grasses. By turning old tracks toward new goals, cities give worn-out places a bright second life.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, the word "versatile" most nearly means
choices: expensive to build and hard to repair
able to serve many different uses well
narrow enough to block large crowds
designed only for fast bicycle commuters
qs.why: Paragraph 4 defines versatile directly as "able to serve many different uses in one narrow space."

qs.q: Which sentence shows how designers flip the social role of an old rail corridor?
choices: Before planting begins, crews must handle rainwater.
Now workers dig shallow basins that divert runoff away from nearby homes and into rain gardens.
This simple shift helps avert costly flood damage during spring storms.
Designers also try to invert the old role of the tracks: a strip that once split two blocks becomes a green path that links them.
qs.why: This sentence explains how a space that used to separate two blocks now links them together.

ev.text: Designers also try to invert the old role of the tracks: a strip that once split two blocks becomes a green path that links them.

qs.q: What do some residents worry might happen if the new trail is not maintained?
choices: It could go back to being an overgrown lot filled with weeds and trash.
Freight trains could return to the rusted tracks during spring downpours.
Rain gardens could stop draining water away from nearby city basements.
Morning commuters could refuse to share the path with neighborhood families.
qs.why: Paragraph 3 says residents fear that without steady care, the trail "might revert to an overgrown lot full of weeds and litter."

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Old brick train depots should always be torn down because compacted soil ruins every garden.
Public meetings usually stop cities from finishing parks because neighbors cannot agree on parking.
Cities can reshape unused rail lines into multi-use parks by solving drainage and community concerns.
Quiet shaded benches are more important than bike lanes or community gardens in urban planning.
qs.why: The reading explains how cities convert abandoned tracks into useful parks while handling soil, runoff, and public debate.

clues.text: harmful problems like hard soil or poor drainage
a loud public debate in which neighbors argue over costs, parking, and noise
able to serve many uses in one tight space
